title: Open Antigravity for the first time
summary: A first launch can ask about your work before it shows the message box. A question with a known answer tells you the app is ready.
where: Use a Google account and the internet. Google lists 64-bit Windows 10, Windows 11, or macOS 13 or newer on a supported Intel or Apple Silicon Mac. Read along on iPad and use the computer for this lesson.
On the download page pick Antigravity App. Google also offers a code editor called an IDE and a version that takes typed commands called a CLI.

actions.title: Find the app
actions.do: In a browser, enter antigravity.google/download in the address box. Choose Antigravity App. Pick the download for your computer.
actions.see: Your browser offers to save a file from Google.
actions.stuck: If you see a command to type, look for the App choice on the download page.

actions.title: Install it
actions.do: Open Downloads. On Windows, open the installer and follow its steps. On Mac, open the downloaded disk image. Drag the app to Applications if the window asks you to.
actions.see: The app appears in Start on Windows or Applications on Mac.
actions.stuck: If the installer says your device is unsupported, compare its download label with your computer’s system details.

actions.title: Sign in
actions.do: Open Antigravity. Follow its Google sign-in screen. After signing in, return to the app window. If a welcome screen asks what kind of work you do, finish that step to reach Home.
actions.see: The Home screen offers a box for your first message.
actions.stuck: If you are still looking at a browser tab, switch back to the Antigravity app.

actions.title: Check a first answer
actions.do: At Home, type “What is 7 plus 5? Reply with one number.” Send the message. Add the numbers yourself.
actions.see: The answer should be 12. You just tested the app with a question you can check.
actions.stuck: If it asks you to choose a folder, return to Home. The next lesson shows how to add one.

roles: Ask what a word in a mail report means.
Explain a word in a team notice.
Talk through a first app idea.

title: Give an agent one folder to work in
summary: Make a folder, create one file in it and open the actual file yourself.
where: Use Antigravity App on Mac or Windows. A folder on your own computer is enough. You can do this exercise without a GitHub account.

actions.title: Make a home for the file
actions.do: Open Finder on Mac or File Explorer on Windows. In Documents, make a new folder called AI Practice. Open the folder and check that it is empty.
actions.see: The top of the window says AI Practice. The folder has no files yet.
actions.stuck: If Documents already has that name, use AI Practice Two for this lesson.

actions.title: Pick the folder
actions.do: In Antigravity's left side bar, choose New Project. Its icon is a folder with a plus. Choose Add Folder, select your practice folder and choose Create.
actions.see: The project shows the name of the folder you picked.
actions.stuck: If it shows Documents, go back and pick just the folder inside it.

actions.title: Ask for one line
actions.do: In the project chat, type “Make welcome.txt in this folder. Put only Welcome aboard on the first line.” Send it.
actions.see: The helper reports that it wrote a file called welcome.txt.
actions.stuck: If the reply only shows a sample on screen, ask it to save the sample as a file in this project.

actions.title: Open the file
actions.do: Go back to the folder in Finder or File Explorer. Open welcome.txt and read the words there.
actions.see: The file itself says Welcome aboard. That is stronger evidence than a chat saying Done.
actions.stuck: If the folder is empty, check the project folder name and let the app finish the saved edit.

roles: Keep a fake mail report in its own folder.
Draft a pretend notice for a team.
Create the first file in a book app.

title: Read a plan before a helper builds a page
summary: Plan a packing list, add a missing item and try the page that the helper makes.
where: On Mac or Windows, open Antigravity App. Stay online and choose an empty practice project.

actions.title: Ask for a plan
actions.do: In the project chat, type “/plan Make one page with checkboxes for Passport and Charger. Show the plan before changing files.” Send your message.
actions.see: A plan card appears. It describes the page the helper wants to make.
actions.stuck: If it writes a whole page right away, start a fresh practice chat. Choose the plan option and ask it to wait.

actions.title: Read the plan card
actions.do: Open the plan card. Look for a page file and the names of both checkboxes. Imagine how you will test it.
actions.see: You can point to Passport and Charger in the proposed work.
actions.stuck: If an item is missing, name it in a comment or in the project chat.

actions.title: Add one item
actions.do: Ask for Earplugs as a third checkbox. Ask to see the new plan before any file edit begins.
actions.see: The plan now lists three separate items.
actions.stuck: If the plan has a note about Earplugs but the list still has only two items, ask to update the list itself.

actions.title: Build and play with it
actions.do: Choose Proceed if shown, or ask the helper to carry out the plan. Open its HTML page in your browser. Check Charger and then clear it.
actions.see: Three boxes appear. Charger changes twice while the other two keep their state.
actions.stuck: If the page shows plain text squares, ask for real clickable checkboxes. Open the changed page and try again.

roles: Plan a report that only reads mail data.
Plan a small change to a staff guide.
List the parts of a form before building it.

title: Find the line a helper changed
summary: Read two versions of a sign. Check the one line you asked the helper to change.
where: Use the Antigravity App on a computer. Open a practice project. The Agent Edits view is where you can inspect one conversation’s changes.

actions.title: Make the sign
actions.do: In the project chat, ask for sign.txt with Harbor Notes on the first line and Dock 3 on the next. Open it and read both lines.
actions.see: You have a two-line file and you know what it said before the edit.
actions.stuck: If the words share one line, ask for a line break after Notes.

actions.title: Change one thing
actions.do: Send “Change Dock 3 to Dock 4 in sign.txt. Keep the title exactly the same.” Wait for the edit.
actions.see: The helper names sign.txt as the file it changed.
actions.stuck: If it changed other files, pause and open the change list before asking for more work.

actions.title: Open the change view
actions.do: In the conversation's Overview panel, choose Review. Choose Agent Edits, then sign.txt. Use Toggle Overview Panel at the top right if the panel is hidden.
actions.see: You can compare the old Dock 3 line with the new Dock 4 line.
actions.stuck: If earlier edits are listed too, open the entry for this file and check the line text before commenting.

actions.title: Check a second edit
actions.do: Comment on that line, or type “Change Dock 4 to Dock 5 on line two.” Open sign.txt again.
actions.see: The title still says Harbor Notes. Line two now says Dock 5.
actions.stuck: If the chat says the edit is done but you still see 4, reopen the saved file in the practice folder.

roles: Check a correction in a mail guide.
Read an edited date in a team notice.
Check one title change in a book app.

title: Open Google AI Studio and run a tiny test
summary: A price card makes a simple first test. When the quantity changes, you can check the total yourself.
where: Use a browser on a Mac or PC. On iPad, turn Safari sideways for extra room. Use an internet connection.
Google limits AI Studio to eligible accounts, regions and adults 18 and older. Work or school rules may also limit it. A younger reader can solve the samples on paper or watch an eligible adult.

actions.title: Go to the address
actions.do: In the browser address box, type aistudio.google.com and press Enter or Go. Use the Google account that has access.
actions.see: You see AI Studio or its account screen.
actions.stuck: If you see search results, type the full address again. A message about age or access means your account cannot use this tool.

actions.title: Open Playground
actions.do: Choose Playground in the menu, unless it is already open. Choose a model that can answer text. A model is the part that makes the answer.
actions.see: There is a box for your question and a Run control.
actions.stuck: If you see an app and a preview, look for Playground in the main menu.

actions.title: Try two cards
actions.do: Enter “One card costs 4 dollars. I buy two. Give the total in dollars.” Choose Run. Add 4 and 4 yourself.
actions.see: The answer should be 8 dollars.
actions.stuck: If the answer includes sales tax, tell it to use only the price and number of cards given.

actions.title: Try three cards
actions.do: Start a fresh Playground chat. Change two cards to three and choose Run again.
actions.see: The answer changes to 12 dollars. The price per card stays 4 dollars.
actions.stuck: If 8 comes back, read your new message. Check that it says three before running it again.

roles: Try a short reply to a fake mail question.
Read a date from a made-up team notice.
Check a score rule for a puzzle.
sources: Google · supported regions and age requirements

title: Give a chat one rule to follow
summary: Set a rule once. See if the helper follows it when the next ticket has no color written on it.
where: Use AI Studio Playground in a browser with an eligible account. The settings are easier to see in a wide window. On iPad, try turning the screen sideways.

actions.title: Find the rule box
actions.do: Start a new Playground chat. Open Run settings at the top right. Find System Instructions. This box holds rules for the chat.
actions.see: You can see the rule box and a separate box for ordinary messages.
actions.stuck: If settings are hidden, widen the window or reopen the controls at the top right.

actions.title: Write one rule
actions.do: In System Instructions, put “Answer with the color word only. If the card gives no color, answer UNKNOWN.” Leave this rule there.
actions.see: The rule remains in place as you move to the normal message box.
actions.stuck: If it appears inside the conversation as a question, move it to System Instructions.

actions.title: Try a clear case
actions.do: In the ordinary box, write “The ticket is blue.” Choose Run. Compare the reply with the stated rule.
actions.see: A correct reply is just blue.
actions.stuck: If it gives a whole sentence, check that you saved the rule in the chat you are using.

actions.title: Try a missing color
actions.do: In that same chat, send “This new ticket has no printed color.” Look first for a color on this ticket alone.
actions.see: The answer should be UNKNOWN. Blue belonged to the earlier ticket.
actions.stuck: If the helper remembers blue, add “Use only the ticket in this turn” to the rule and test both tickets again.

roles: Give each mail slip the same kind of label.
Use the same labels for each team form.
Make a word game give one-word answers.

title: Make a working score counter in Build
summary: Describe a small app, use its real buttons and ask for a change you can test.
where: Open aistudio.google.com/apps on a computer with eligible AI Studio access. Stay online to build the page. A wide window leaves space for the chat and the app preview.

actions.title: Find Build
actions.do: Go to AI Studio and choose Build, or open aistudio.google.com/apps. Choose to start a new app from a prompt.
actions.see: You see a place to describe the app you want to make.
actions.stuck: If your screen shows Playground, return to the main menu and open Build.

actions.title: Describe the buttons
actions.do: Send “Make a score counter for a browser. Start at zero. Add one increases the score by 1. Reset returns it to 0. Use big numbers. Let it work without a login.”
actions.see: The preview shows a score of 0 and both buttons.
actions.stuck: If the builder gives only a description, ask it to make and show the working page.

actions.title: Try the preview
actions.do: Click Add one two times and look at the score after each click. Click Reset.
actions.see: The numbers go 1, 2, then 0. You have tested both buttons on the running page.
actions.stuck: If the number freezes, tell Build which button you pressed and the number it should show.

actions.title: Ask for a change
actions.do: Ask for a Subtract one button that allows negative scores. From zero, press it once. Try Reset again.
actions.see: The new button gives -1. Reset still gives 0.
actions.stuck: If it stops at zero, tell the builder that a penalty can put the score less than zero. Retest the three buttons.

roles: Build a fake mail-ticket counter.
Try a count field for a shared list.
Make a score button for a card game.

title: Open Gemini and ask a second question
summary: A chat can use facts from the turn before. Check its memory with a small packing problem.
where: On iPad use Google Gemini from Google in the App Store, or open gemini.google.com in Safari. The website also works on Mac and PC. Use an account that may access Gemini.

actions.title: Open Gemini
actions.do: On iPad, search the App Store for Google Gemini. Choose Google's listing and tap Get or Open. In a browser, enter gemini.google.com.
actions.see: Gemini opens or asks you to sign in.
actions.stuck: If a search turns up several apps with similar names, check who publishes the app.

actions.title: Check the account
actions.do: Sign in if asked. Open the profile picture and check the account. Return to the main screen and start a new chat.
actions.see: A blank place to enter your question is ready.
actions.stuck: If the account is managed by a school or a workplace, the features on it may differ. Use an account approved for the exercise.

actions.title: Give it the facts
actions.do: Send “I packed two red shirts and one blue shirt. How many shirts is that? Use only these facts.” Count the shirts before you read the reply.
actions.see: The answer is three shirts.
actions.stuck: If it gives an outfit list, ask again for just the total number of shirts.

actions.title: Change one fact
actions.do: Stay in this chat. Send “I take out one red shirt. How many red and blue shirts remain?”
actions.see: One red and one blue remain. Together that makes two.
actions.stuck: If you started a new chat by mistake, paste the original shirt counts again before asking about the change.

roles: Summarize a pretend mail support note.
Rewrite one sentence from a team notice.
Plan a simple feature on an iPad.

title: Give Gemini one small task to finish
summary: Let Gemini make a three-line plan. Check the times in the finished work before you use it.
where: Use Gemini on the web or in its mobile app while online. Age, region, account and rollout can affect access.
Look for Task in the message composer. Older guides call this feature Spark. You can try the math in an ordinary chat if your account has no Task choice.

actions.title: Choose Task
actions.do: Start a new Gemini chat. Select Task in the composer. Look at the model menu. Leave the current choice in place.
actions.see: The message area shows you are starting a task.
actions.stuck: If the option is missing, use an ordinary chat to try the sample. The separate progress view requires Task access.

actions.title: Set one job
actions.do: Send “Make a one-page schedule from these facts. The dock opens at 08:00. Boarding starts at 09:15. Leave 30 minutes before the dock opens. Put all three in time order.”
actions.see: Gemini starts work with enough facts to figure out the departure time.
actions.stuck: If it asks which dock or day, say this is a pretend schedule and the three given times are all you need.

actions.title: Peek at progress
actions.do: Open the task from Menu. Tap its progress chip or choose Task progress at the top.
actions.see: You can see progress or that the task has finished.
actions.stuck: If you see a different conversation, return to Menu and find the one with the dock schedule.

actions.title: Read what it made
actions.do: Open the finished text or file. Count back half an hour from 08:00. Check the order of all three lines.
actions.see: Leave at 07:30, dock opens at 08:00 and board at 09:15.
actions.stuck: If it says 08:45, show which event the half hour belongs to. Ask it to count back from dock opening.

roles: Draft a pretend mail-check schedule.
Put steps for a team change in time order.
Plan the stops for a travel app.
sources: Google · create tasks on iPhone and iPad
Google · Tasks in Gemini, formerly Spark

title: Follow a research answer back to its sources
summary: Ask Gemini to compare two public pages. Then open each one and decide whether the answer matches it.
where: Use Gemini online on an iPad, Mac or PC with Deep Research available to your account. This exercise uses public help pages.

actions.title: Choose Deep Research
actions.do: Start a new chat. Open the tools menu beside the message box. On iPad, look under Add files or tools. Choose Deep Research.
actions.see: Gemini offers to plan a research task.
actions.stuck: If your account lacks the tool, practice opening two public sources and comparing them yourself.

actions.title: Ask a narrow question
actions.do: Ask “Use the official desktop and iPad help pages for Gemini Notebook. Give me one way to add a source that works on both. Link one page for each device.” Before starting, read the plan.
actions.see: The plan calls for two help pages and one shared task. The result will have a clear test.
actions.stuck: If the plan wanders into model prices or reviews, ask it to compare only the steps for adding a source.

actions.title: Start the search
actions.do: Choose Start research. When Gemini reports that the work is ready, return to the conversation and choose Open.
actions.see: The finished report has a claim and links you can follow.
actions.stuck: If there is only a plan, use Start research. A plan describes work that has yet to happen.

actions.title: Check the links
actions.do: Open the two cited help pages. On each page find the part that explains how to add a source. Could you use the proposed method on both devices?
actions.see: You can point to the steps on both pages, or say which page does not support the method the report picked.
actions.stuck: If a link goes to a general home page, request a direct help page for that device. Read the steps yourself.

roles: Compare two public guides to a mail feature.
Check the source of a team software claim.
Find evidence for a science quiz.
sources: Google · Deep Research on iPhone and iPad

title: Make a notebook from two short notes
summary: Give Gemini Notebook two sources. Open a source yourself to check where an answer came from. This tool was once called NotebookLM.
where: Use an eligible account. Open Gemini Notebook on your computer or its app on iPad if available. Make a fresh notebook so you know exactly which sources it has.

actions.title: Make a notebook
actions.do: Open the notebook list. Select Create new or New notebook. Name it Ferry Day. Think of it as a small binder for this trip.
actions.see: The notebook has a name and an area where sources will go.
actions.stuck: If you see a regular Gemini chat, open the notebook area or the separate Gemini Notebook app.

actions.title: Put in two notes
actions.do: Add two sources as pasted text or files. Name the first Schedule and give it “Meet at Pier 6 at 9:15.” Name the second Packing and give it “Bring a hat and a notebook.”
actions.see: Two separate entries show up. Open each one and check its words.
actions.stuck: If paste is unavailable, save each note as a short text file and use the upload control.

actions.title: Follow the source
actions.do: Ask “Which pier should I use? What should I bring? Show the source for each answer.” Open the little source link beside each answer.
actions.see: Pier 6 comes from Schedule. The hat and notebook come from Packing.
actions.stuck: If it points to the wrong note, ask one question at a time. Read the linked words before trusting the answer.

actions.title: Ask a missing question
actions.do: Ask “How much does the ticket cost?” Read the two notes yourself and check whether either gives a fare.
actions.see: The price is unknown from these sources. A fare notice could fill in the missing fact.
actions.stuck: If the reply gives an amount, ask to see the price in the original note. Treat it as unknown unless you can find those words.

roles: Keep two public mail guides together and compare them.
Study a practice agenda beside its meeting notes.
Write app help from its actual list of features.
